overview: This card concerns medieval Serbian principalities, the Nemanjic kingdom and empire, and later successor lordships. Their borders and institutions changed over time. Quarry settlements, burnt food, fish bones, illuminated books and a seal-maker's tool reveal work and learning beyond royal campaigns. Evidence from a monastery or court describes that setting, not every household.

periods.title: Principalities between larger powers
periods.summary: Early Serbian principalities experienced changing relations with Bulgaria and Byzantium. Their shifting political geography should not be equated with the borders of modern Serbia.

periods.title: Nemanjic patronage and monastic building
periods.summary: Stefan Nemanja's family consolidated power during the later twelfth century. Studenica joined royal patronage to marble quarrying, stone carving and religious life.

periods.title: A kingdom and its institutions
periods.summary: Stefan received a royal crown in 1217; an independent Serbian archbishopric followed in 1219. Mining settlements and trading centres became important to the kingdom.

periods.title: Empire and regional power
periods.summary: Dusan took the imperial title in 1346. Regional lords gained greater independence under his successor Uros, whose death in 1371 ended Nemanjic imperial rule.

periods.title: Successor lordships and despotate
periods.summary: Regional rulers maintained courts, mining centres and monasteries as the political landscape fragmented. The later despotate developed new capitals, including Smederevo beside the Danube.

items.text: Near Studenica, marble quarries and remains of a workers' settlement connect the Church of the Virgin with the people who extracted and shaped its stone. The monastery's finely finished surfaces depended on a wider landscape of skilled and demanding labour.

Studenica's Church of the Virgin combines a domed interior with an exterior drawing on Romanesque architecture. Its design became a model for other monasteries. Builders adapted forms circulating across the Adriatic and Byzantine worlds rather than working within a sealed national tradition.

Paintings made in the Church of the Virgin in 1208 and 1209 organise religious figures through expressive gestures and carefully conceived space. Their surviving setting lets historians study images as part of a building used for worship, rather than as detached museum pictures.

Charred remains from twelfth- and thirteenth-century buildings at Ras include bread wheat, rye, barley, oats and millet. Wheat was most abundant in the studied samples. Weeds mixed with grain, including corncockle, preserve traces of crop handling as well as the crops themselves.

The Ras study also identified a round piece of burnt bread, cereal remains in a pot and fragments of peach stones. These finds bring prepared food and fruit into view. They document particular deposits, not a complete menu or the quantities eaten by every resident.

Waste deposits at Studenica from the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries contained catfish, carp and pike alongside migratory sturgeon. The researchers connect the sturgeon with the distant Danube. Feeding a monastery could involve both nearby fishing and longer supply routes.

Studenica's fish bones preserve information about body parts, size and cutting. The authors suggest that some large fish arrived whole, perhaps dried or salted. Preservation methods are an interpretation of the remains; the bones do not supply a surviving recipe.

sections.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority

items.text: Excavation at Drenje in Rudnik revealed secular buildings and three churches, two Orthodox and one Catholic, in a settlement flourishing during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. These remains suggest a varied religious landscape. Identifying the area specifically as the medieval market remains an interpretation.

A seal-die from a pit at Rudnik bears Prince Lazar's name and a helmet with horned ornament. Dated to his rule there between 1373 and 1389, it is a tool for producing official impressions. No matching impression was known to the study's authors.

sections.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital

items.text: The late twelfth-century Miroslav Gospel combines writing on parchment with gilding and painted decoration. Its illuminations draw on Italian and Byzantine artistic traditions. The manuscript shows bookmaking as a collaboration of textual, material and visual skills shaped by connections beyond one court.

The Miroslav Gospel arranges readings for liturgical use rather than simply presenting an unbroken narrative. Its language and spelling also preserve evidence of a regional scribal tradition. A book could guide repeated communal worship while carrying the choices of the people who copied it.

An embroidered priestly stole, or epitrachelion, from the Church of Saints Peter and Paul near Novi Pazar preserves another demanding craft. The National Museum dates its style to the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. This ceremonial garment cannot stand for ordinary clothing.

Smederevo's new court was built at the meeting of the Danube and Jezava in 1428 to 1430. Its builders faced shortages of local stone, bringing material from farther away and reusing older masonry. The fortress records transport and salvage as well as defensive planning.

ending.text: Ottoman conquest of Smederevo in 1459 ended the remaining Serbian despotate. The medieval empire had fragmented much earlier; 1389 was not the date when all Serbian political institutions vanished. Settlement at Smederevo and religious communities such as Studenica continued under changed conditions. The imported map endpoint of 1300 is not a historical fall date.

sources.note: Starinar 66, pages 161-171, abstract: Drenje buildings, three churches, seal-die in pit 2 and date 1373-1389. Market function and deposition in 1390 are hypotheses, not direct observations.

sources.note: Inscription description: illuminated parchment, Italian and Byzantine artistic influences, evangelistary structure and Rascian orthography. Late twelfth century avoids false precision between catalogue dates.
